book.title: Introduction to Python Programming
book.baseline: General Python 3.9+ syntax and standard library, checked against the Python 3.13 documentation without relying on newer exclusive features. Web execution replays are generated with CPython 3.14; language coverage and replay runtime are recorded separately.
book.audience: Readers with no programming experience. Observe the web replays first, then use Section 1.1 to learn how to save files and run programs.
outcomes: Write a runnable program from an empty file
Understand types, branches, loops, and data containers
Organize functions and handle invalid input
Read and write small text, JSON, and CSV files
Write boundary and integration tests for a command-line project
outOfScope: Concurrency, async, generators, and performance tuning

localSetup: Install the interpreter: open python.org, choose Downloads, and install a supported Python 3 release. The interpreter runs your code. If its command is unavailable, check that installation completed.

Save the code: create a practice folder and a plain-text file in a code editor. Enter the two lines above and save as hello.py. The name must end in .py, not .py.txt. Do not save code as a Word document.

body.title: Numbers and text serve different purposes

lessons.title: Numbers and arithmetic
lessons.subtitle: For the same candies, you can ask for an average or for full bags and leftovers.
lessons.concept: For the same candies, you can ask for an average or for full bags and leftovers.

body.title: Use familiar arithmetic
body.text: Python uses + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, and / for division. For example, 3 * 5 gives 15 and 17 / 5 gives 3.4. Do not quote numbers. print(3 * 5) calculates before displaying. Multiplication and division precede addition and subtraction; use parentheses to change the order, as in (2 + 3) * 4.

body.title: Find full bags and leftovers
body.text: For full bags only, 17 // 5 gives 3. The two slashes perform floor division. For these nonnegative quantities, this is the full-bag count. 17 % 5 gives the remainder 2; here % does not mean percent. Three bags use 15 candies, leaving 17 - 15 = 2.

body.title: Reconstruct the original total
body.text: Multiply full bags by capacity and add leftovers: 3 * 5 + 2 = 17. If 20 candies fit 5 per bag, the remainder is 0. Change the total, then the capacity, one at a time. Counts are nonnegative integers and bag capacity must be positive.

formalDefinition.text: For this nonnegative-integer packing model, // gives full bags and % gives leftovers: bags times capacity plus remainder equals total.
conditions: Counts are nonnegative integers; bag capacity is an integer greater than 0.
The divisor for /, //, and % must not be 0.

derivation.text: total refers to 17 candies; size refers to capacity 5.
Use // to obtain 3 full bags.
Use % to obtain remainder 2; check 3 * 5 + 2 = 17.

The project stores amounts as integer cents; Decimal is an option for later study of decimal arithmetic.

body.title: Turn a question into a condition
body.text: Suppose the fare is 5 and money holds the amount you have. money >= 5 asks whether you have at least 5; >= means greater than or equal to. A comparison returns True or False. Predict the result before following the program.

body.title: Write two paths with if and else
body.text: if condition: starts the path taken when the condition is true; else: starts the other path. After each colon, start a new line and indent the body by four spaces. Indentation groups statements into a branch. This test takes one branch: it cannot print both messages.

body.title: Check the exact boundary
body.text: Try 6, then 4, then exactly 5. The >= comparison includes equality, so 5 is enough. Replacing it with > would reject the exact fare. Use == to compare equality; a single = assigns a value.

formalDefinition.text: An if statement runs its indented body when the condition is true. Otherwise it runs the else body. Only one branch runs.
conditions: Keep the colon and indentation. Use = for assignment and == for equality.

body.title: Print a sequence of numbers
body.text: for number in range(1, 4): gives number the values 1, 2, and 3 in turn. range produces integers: it includes 1 but excludes 4. The indented print(number) runs once per value, producing three lines.

lessons.subtitle: A while loop checks its condition before each iteration. True continues; false stops.
lessons.concept: A while loop checks its condition before each iteration. True continues; false stops.

body.title: Check before each iteration
body.text: while remaining > 0: runs its indented body only while remaining is positive. It tests the condition again on every iteration. A for loop is useful for going through items; a while loop is useful when a condition determines whether to continue.

body.title: Move toward the stopping condition
body.text: remaining = remaining - 1 reduces the value by 1. Starting at 3, it becomes 2, 1, then 0. At 0 the condition is false and the loop stops. Without that update, the condition stays true and the loop repeats indefinitely. Do not run the version with the update removed.

formalDefinition.text: A while loop checks first, runs its body only when the condition is true, then checks again after the body.
conditions: Update the state so the condition eventually becomes false. Verify termination with small inputs first.

lessons.title: Lists and shopping lists
lessons.subtitle: A list stores items in order. Read them by position or process them one by one.
lessons.concept: A list stores items in order. Read them by position or process them one by one.

body.title: Put items inside square brackets
body.text: items = ["apple", "bread"] creates a list with two strings, separated by a comma inside square brackets. Lists preserve order. items[0] retrieves the first item; items[1] retrieves the second. Positions start at 0. len(items) gives the number of items, here 2.

body.title: Append an item, then iterate
body.text: items.append("milk") adds an item at the end. The dot selects an operation on this list; append is its name. for item in items: visits each item directly, without a range or an index.

body.title: Two names can refer to one list
body.text: other = items does not copy the list. It gives the same list another name, so appending through other also changes what items sees. For independent simple lists, use other = items.copy(). This is a shallow copy; here the list contains only strings or numbers.

formalDefinition.text: Lists preserve order and duplicates, and positions start at 0. append adds at the end; copy duplicates the simple, one-level lists used here.
conditions: An index must be within the list. An empty list has no item at index 0.
Here copy() is used on one-level lists of numbers or strings.

body.text: prices = {"apple": 3, "bread": 5} is a dictionary. Each pair has a key on the left and its value on the right. A colon joins them; commas separate pairs. prices["apple"] retrieves 3 by key. These square brackets contain a key, not a list position.

body.title: Add and update by key
body.text: prices["milk"] = 4 adds a new product; prices["apple"] = 6 updates an existing price. Each key has one current value. for name in prices: visits the keys; prices[name] retrieves the corresponding value.

body.title: Choose a default for a missing key
body.text: Indexing a missing key raises KeyError. prices.get("rice", 0) retrieves the value if present and returns 0 otherwise, without inserting rice. This is useful for counting: counts[name] = counts.get(name, 0) + 1 starts an unseen item at 0 and adds one.

formalDefinition.text: A dictionary maps keys to values. Square brackets read an existing key; get can supply a default for a missing key.
conditions: A key must exist for direct indexed lookup. For a missing key, get lets you choose a default.

lessons.title: Tuples and sets: records and distinct values
lessons.subtitle: Use a tuple for a fixed record and a set when you care which values occur.
lessons.concept: Use a tuple for a fixed record and a set when you care which values occur.

body.title: Group a fixed pair of values
body.text: point = (3, 4) creates a tuple using parentheses. As with a list, point[0] gives 3 and point[1] gives 4, but tuple positions cannot be reassigned. A tuple suits a fixed record such as coordinates. Here we use pairs; a one-item tuple needs a comma: (3,).

body.title: Keep each distinct value once
body.text: cities = {"Beijing", "Shanghai", "Beijing"} is a set. It keeps each distinct value once, so len(cities) is 2. With no colons, these are not dictionary key-value pairs. An empty set is set(); {} is an empty dictionary.

body.title: Choose a container for the task
body.text: "Beijing" in cities tests membership. A set has no first or second position and promises no display order. Use sorted(cities) for a consistently ordered list. Choose a list for order and duplicates, a dictionary for key-value lookup, a tuple for a fixed record, and a set for distinct values and membership.

formalDefinition.text: Tuple positions cannot be reassigned. A set keeps distinct values, and in tests membership.
conditions: Set elements must be hashable. This lesson uses only numbers and strings.
Sets do not support positional indexing or guarantee display order.

body.title: Start with a familiar for loop
body.text: Starting with values = [1, 2, 3], create result = []. In a loop, calculate value * 2 and add it with result.append(...). The result is [2, 4, 6]. The original remains [1, 2, 3] because the additions went into a new list.

body.title: Express the same steps in one line
body.text: result = [value * 2 for value in values] expresses the same simple process. Read the for clause first: take each value from values. Then read value * 2: what each item becomes. The surrounding brackets collect those results into a list.

body.title: Add a filter when needed
body.text: [value * 2 for value in values if value >= 2] keeps values at least 2, then doubles them, giving [4, 6]. Check a small list by hand. For nested loops or complicated conditions, an ordinary for loop may be clearer. The goal is to explain each result, not to minimize line count.

formalDefinition.text: [expression for item in data if condition] filters items, evaluates an expression, and collects the results in a new list. The condition is optional.
conditions: Each example runs independently from the beginning. Start with the stated inputs, then change one thing.

lessons.title: Functions, parameters, and return values
lessons.subtitle: Name a reusable sequence of steps, give it input when calling it, and capture its result.
lessons.concept: Name a reusable sequence of steps, give it input when calling it, and capture its result.
lessons.intuition: A doubling machine takes 3 and returns 6.
objectives: Call the function and capture its result

body.title: Give the steps a name
body.text: def double(number): defines a function named double. A function is a reusable sequence of steps; number names its input and is called a parameter. The indented return number * 2 doubles it and sends the result to the caller. Defining the function records the steps; it does not yet compute with 3.

body.title: Call the function and capture its result

body.title: Handle the expected failure with try and except

body.title: Calculate expectations independently

body.title: Cover ordinary and boundary cases
body.text: Passing for 3 is not enough. Try 0, negative inputs, and values that expose likely bugs. formalDefinition.text: A test compares an actual result with an independently determined expectation. assert requires its condition to be true.
